533.title: Your faith has made you well (Luke 8:40–56)
533.hook: a bleeding woman and a dying girl, twelve years each
533.howItsDone: Some Christians pray with the healing of the woman and Jairus's daughter when they or someone they love is ill, and in some churches prayer for the sick includes a gentle touch on the shoulder or hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a storm stilled, a man sent home, and your line, return to your house.

Twelve years ties today's two stories together. Jairus, a ruler of the local synagogue, an important man in town, falls at Jesus' feet. His only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying. Jesus goes, and the crowd presses so tightly it's hard to move. Somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody notices, who has been bleeding for twelve years: as long as Jairus's daughter has been alive. Luke says she had spent everything she had on doctors, and none could heal her. She doesn't ask for anything. She has a plan.

Under the law of her time, her bleeding made her ritually unclean, and for twelve years that would have kept her at the edges of worship and of ordinary touch. She comes up from behind and, in the King James words, "touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched." She just wants to slip away. But Jesus stops. "Who touched me?" Peter points out that the whole crowd is pressing against him. But Jesus says, "Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me." Virtue here means power. Trembling, she comes forward and tells everything in front of everyone. And Jesus says: "Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace." Daughter: a family word for a woman kept at the edges, said in public, so the whole town hears she is well. Made thee whole is the Greek sozo, the same phrase as "thy faith hath saved thee" at Simon's dinner. Healed and saved share one word. But the stop has cost time. A messenger arrives: "Thy daughter is dead; trouble not the Master." Jesus says: "Fear not: believe only, and she shall be made whole." At the house, the mourners are wailing. He says she's sleeping, and they laugh at him. He takes her hand: "Maid, arise." She gets up. And then a very practical line: he tells them to give her something to eat.
screen: `SHE TOUCHED THE BORDER OF HIS GARMENT.`
`DAUGHTER: THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`
then, large: `FEAR NOT: BELIEVE ONLY, AND SHE SHALL BE MADE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people who need help right now: one loud about it, like Jairus, urgent and asking, and one quiet, like the woman in the crowd, hoping nobody notices. Notice which one your attention runs to first, then bring the other forward too; in the story, Jesus stops for the woman and still reaches the girl. If you pray, you can hold both before God together; if you don't, simply keep both in your care.
Sozo, the Greek word used for both healing and being saved: Jesus' words to a woman healed after twelve years, said on the way to a twelve-year-old girl he raises with a word, maid, arise.
Your line: only believe. There was room on that road for both of them. See you tomorrow.

534.title: The twelve sent out (Luke 9:1–17)
534.hook: sent with nothing, then the five thousand fed
534.carry: you give them something to eat
534.howItsDone: Some Christian food pantries and church meal programs take "give ye them to eat" as a motto, and Christians often notice in this meal the actions of the Last Supper and communion: taking, blessing, breaking and giving bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a woman in the crowd, a girl who rose and ate, and your line, only believe.

No walking stick, no bag, no bread, no money, no spare clothes. That's the packing list Jesus gives the twelve. In the King James words: "Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money; neither have two coats apiece." A scrip is a traveler's bag. They go out empty-handed, village by village, to preach and to heal, depending on whoever opens a door. Until now they've watched; now they're sent. And word spreads so far that Herod himself, who had John beheaded, hears and is perplexed. Who is this? He wants to see him.
screen: `NO STAFF, NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.`

segments.voice: The twelve come back full of stories, and Jesus takes them aside privately, to a deserted place near a town called Bethsaida. The crowds follow. Luke says Jesus "received them," spoke about the kingdom, and healed those who needed it. The sun gets low. And the twelve, sensibly, say: "Send the multitude away, that they may go into the towns and country round about, and lodge, and get victuals: for we are here in a desert place." It's a reasonable plan. Jesus answers, short and plain: "Give ye them to eat." You feed them. They've just come back from a journey where they carried nothing; now he hands the problem back to them. They count: "We have no more but five loaves and two fishes." About five thousand men, Luke says. Jesus has them sit in groups of about fifty, like guests at a meal. He takes the loaves and fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives to the disciples to set before the crowd. Later, at the Last Supper, nearly the same movements return: took, gave thanks, broke, gave. Everyone eats and is filled, and they pick up twelve baskets of leftovers. Some readers notice: one for each of the twelve who said send them away. Jesus didn't do it without them. He did it through their hands, with what they already had, which was almost nothing.
screen: then, large: `GIVE YE THEM TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Think of one small comfort you could set aside for a day, the second coffee, the show, the scrolling before sleep, not as punishment but to notice how much you usually carry. Then picture what that small saving of money or time could become in someone else's hands: a meal, a gift, an hour. If you pray, you can offer that small thing to God; if you don't, simply decide where it goes.
Scrip, an old word for a traveler's bag: Jesus sends the twelve out with nothing, then hands them a hungry crowd and five loaves, and through their hands five thousand are fed.
Your line: you give them something to eat. Almost nothing, in their hands, fed a crowd. Day five hundred thirty-four.

535.title: Daily cross (Luke 9:18–27)
535.hook: Luke adds one word: take up your cross daily
535.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of "carrying their cross" for the ordinary burdens of daily life, and in many traditions the daily offering of one's day to God is a morning practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five loaves, five thousand fed, and your line, you give them something to eat.

Matthew, Mark and Luke all record the same hard saying: if anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself and take up his cross. But Luke's version has one extra word, easy to miss, and once you see it, the whole sentence changes shape. It comes after a quiet moment: Jesus was "alone praying," with only his disciples nearby. Prayer at a turning point, again. When he finishes, he asks the kind of question you'd ask your closest friends late at night, when the crowd has gone home: "Whom say the people that I am?"
screen: `WHOM SAY THE PEOPLE THAT I AM?`

segments.voice: They report the talk: John the Baptist, back from the dead; Elijah; one of the old prophets. Then: "But whom say ye that I am?" Peter answers: "The Christ of God." Christ means anointed one, the Messiah, the king Israel hoped for. Jesus tells them not to spread it, and says something nobody expected a Messiah to say: "The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and be raised the third day." Then, to everyone: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." Daily. In Greek, kath hemeran, day by day. Matthew and Mark don't have it. In Rome's world, a cross wasn't a symbol. It was how the empire executed rebels and slaves, and the condemned man carried the crossbeam through the streets. Taking up your cross meant walking toward the end. Matthew and Mark say it like a single great decision; Luke adds daily, and it becomes a thing you pick up again every morning. Christians have heard it both ways at once. Some have faced death for their faith. Most have faced the ordinary kind: putting someone else first again today, keeping a promise again today. "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it." In Luke, losing your life happens one day at a time.
screen: `WHOM SAY YE? THE CHRIST OF GOD.`
then, large: `TAKE UP HIS CROSS DAILY, AND FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Think about the ordinary weight that's yours to pick up every day, caring for a parent, a hard job, patience with a child or with your own body, and see it plainly, no bigger and no smaller than it is. Picture tomorrow morning, picking it up again on purpose, with a little love in it. If you pray, you can offer that daily weight to God; if you don't, simply choose to carry it with care.
Daily cross. Peter names Jesus the Christ of God, and Jesus says anyone who follows him must take up the cross, and Luke adds the word daily.
Your line: daily. Not one great moment, but every morning, again. That's day five hundred thirty-five.

536.title: His face shone (Luke 9:28–36)
536.hook: he was praying when his face changed; Moses and Elijah talk of his departure
536.howItsDone: Churches in several traditions keep a feast of the Transfiguration, and some Protestant churches mark Transfiguration Sunday just before Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Peter's answer, a cross picked up every morning, and your line, daily.

About eight days after the talk of the cross, Jesus takes three friends, Peter, John and James, and climbs a mountain. Luke tells us why: they went up "to pray." Some people describe a place, a hospital chapel, a hilltop, a kitchen at 4am, where they sat in prayer or silence long enough that something in the room seemed to shift. The three disciples are tired; Luke says they were "heavy with sleep." And while they fight to keep their eyes open, Jesus keeps praying. Then his face begins to change.

In the King James words: "And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glistering." As he prayed: that's Luke's own emphasis. Matthew says his face did shine as the sun; Luke says it changed while he was praying. The light comes in the middle of prayer. Then two men are talking with him, Moses and Elijah, the lawgiver and the prophet. In Exodus, Moses' own face shone after he spoke with God on a mountain. And what are they talking about? They "spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem." Decease, in Greek, is exodos: a departure, a way out. Some readers hear in it the book of Exodus, Moses leading Israel out of slavery. Here, beside Moses, Jesus talks about his own exodus, the death and rising waiting for him in Jerusalem. Peter wakes enough to say something: "Master, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles." Three shelters. Stay, make it last. Luke adds kindly that he didn't know what he was saying. Then a cloud covers them, and a voice: "This is my beloved Son: hear him." When the cloud lifts, Jesus is alone, and they tell no one in those days. Churches remember this as the Transfiguration, the change of form. But in Luke, the change doesn't come from nowhere. It comes while he prays.
screen: then, large: `AS HE PRAYED, THE FASHION OF HIS COUNTENANCE WAS ALTERED.`

segments.voice: Don't aim for a vision; aim for staying, past the point where you'd normally stop, through the noisy first minute of lists and worries and tiredness. Notice if something softens, a thought loosening, your shoulders dropping, and don't grab at it, the way Peter wanted to build shelters. If you pray, you can let the words run out and simply stay; if you don't, simply stay.
Exodos, Greek for a going out, a departure: on a mountain, while Jesus prays, his face changes, and Moses and Elijah speak with him about his coming death and rising at Jerusalem.
Your line: while he prayed. The light came in the middle of the praying. Day five hundred thirty-six, done.

537.title: Whoever is least (Luke 9:37–50)
537.hook: a boy healed, an argument about greatness, a child set beside him
537.howItsDone: Some churches point to Luke 9:48 in their work with children, from Sunday schools to child-protection and welcome policies, as a sign that receiving a child is receiving Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a changed face on the mountain, and your line, while he prayed.

The next day they come down the mountain to a crowd, and a father shouting over the noise: "Master, I beseech thee, look upon my son: for he is mine only child." Luke says a spirit seizes the boy, throws him into convulsions and leaves him bruised. And the father adds the painful part: "I besought thy disciples to cast him out; and they could not." The disciples who stayed below have failed in front of everyone. Jesus' answer is weary, almost a sigh at the whole generation: how long shall I be with you? Then, simply: "Bring thy son hither."
screen: `LOOK UPON MY SON: MINE ONLY CHILD.`

segments.voice: Even as the boy comes, he's thrown down again. Jesus rebukes the spirit, heals the child, and, in the King James words, "delivered him again to his father." Gave him back, the same gesture as the widow's son at Nain. The crowd is "amazed at the mighty power of God." While everyone marvels, Jesus tells his disciples something hard: the Son of man will be delivered into human hands. They don't understand, and they're afraid to ask. Then, Luke says, "there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest." Right after failing to heal a boy. Right after hearing their teacher will be handed over. Jesus knows what they're thinking, and answers without a speech. He "took a child, and set him by him." Next to himself. They've been arguing about rank, and a child has none to offer. "Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great." Then John, a little too quickly: we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we stopped him, because he isn't one of us. Jesus: "Forbid him not: for he that is not against us is for us." Two lessons in a row against the same instinct: to rank people, and to guard the circle.
screen: then, large: `HE THAT IS LEAST AMONG YOU ALL, THE SAME SHALL BE GREAT.`

segments.voice: Picture Jesus setting a child next to him while the grown-ups go quiet, then think of a child in your life: your own, a neighbor's kid, a student, or the child you once were. Let one need come clearly that's easy to overlook when adult things feel urgent: time, a ride, a bedtime story, a promise kept. If you pray, you can hold that child before God; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with care.
John. One of the twelve, who tried to stop a stranger driving out demons in Jesus' name, and was told forbid him not, on the day Jesus set a child beside him.
Your line: the least is the greatest. A child with no rank gets the seat beside him. See you tomorrow.

538.title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
538.hook: he turns toward Jerusalem; foxes have holes, but he has nowhere to lay his head
538.howItsDone: Commentators call this long stretch of Luke the travel narrative, and some Christians read through it slowly, a few verses a day, as a journey toward Jerusalem and Holy Week.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a child set beside Jesus while the disciples argued about rank, and your line, the least is the greatest.

Halfway through chapter nine, Luke's Gospel turns a corner, and you can almost feel the road tilt. In the King James words: "when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." From here on, Jesus is walking. The Good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus in the tree: Luke sets them on the road to Jerusalem, where Jesus has already said what is waiting. Some readers hear an echo of Isaiah, where God's servant says: "therefore have I set my face like a flint." Flint. Hard stone. Not stubbornness. Resolve.

The road goes through Samaria first. In John's Gospel, a Samaritan woman names one old dispute between Samaritans and Jews: where to worship. Jesus sends messengers ahead to find a place to stay, and a Samaritan village turns them away, Luke says, because he was heading to Jerusalem. James and John are furious: "Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?" And Luke says: "he turned, and rebuked them." They simply go to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you anywhere. Jesus: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Anywhere includes nowhere. To the second, Jesus says: follow me. The man says, let me first go and bury my father. Jesus: "Let the dead bury their dead." Readers differ: some think the father had just died, others that the man meant to wait until his father died someday. The text doesn't say. What's clear is the urgency. The third says, let me first say goodbye to my family. And Jesus answers: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Look back over your shoulder and the furrow goes crooked. You keep your eyes on a point ahead, and walk toward it.
screen: `HAND TO THE PLOUGH, NO LOOKING BACK.`
then, large: `HE STEDFASTLY SET HIS FACE TO GO TO JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you keep circling and not doing, a hard conversation, a doctor's appointment, an apology, and notice the let-me-first voices, the someday. Picture a plowman with his eyes on the far side of the field, and your own face set toward that one thing, calm and steady, then choose the very first step. If you pray, you can ask for a steady face; if you don't, simply fix your eyes on the step.
Flint, the hard stone Isaiah uses for an unbending resolve: Luke's turning point, where Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem and will not be turned back.
Your line: no looking back. The furrow runs straight when your eyes stay ahead. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

539.title: Seventy sent (Luke 10:1–20)
539.hook: sent in pairs: say peace to this house first
539.howItsDone: In the Book of Common Prayer, the order for the visitation of the sick opens with "Peace be to this house," and some Christians use the same words when blessing a home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, flint: Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem, and your line was no looking back.

What's the first thing you say when you walk into someone's home? Hi. Sorry I'm late. Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem now, and he sends out a much bigger group than the twelve. In the King James words: "the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come." Two by two, so no one goes alone. Ahead of him, preparing the way. And first, he tells them exactly what to say at the door.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY AT THE DOOR?`

segments.voice: First, the honest warning: "The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few." And: "behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves." Not soldiers. Lambs. The packing list is lighter than ever: no purse, no bag, no shoes, and no stopping to chat with everyone on the road. Then the doorway: "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house." Behind the Greek word for peace stands the Hebrew greeting shalom, which reaches past the absence of fighting toward wholeness and well-being. Then a beautiful detail: "And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again." Peace is like something you set down in a room. If someone there is open to it, it stays. If not, it comes back to you; you don't lose it by offering it. Stay in one house, he says. Eat what they put in front of you. Heal the sick. Say the kingdom of God has come near. And if a town won't welcome you, shake off the dust and move on. The seventy come back overjoyed: even the demons obey us in your name! Jesus gently turns their joy: "rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." Not in the power they had, but in being known by name. Luke never names them; they aren't the twelve.
screen: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`
then, large: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a home you'll walk into soon: your own after work, a friend's, a parent's, maybe one where things are tense or simply tired. Picture yourself at the door bringing peace in before a word about traffic or dinner, like setting down a gift, and then letting go of whether it's received. If you pray, say the line from Luke silently at the door; if you don't, simply bring calm in with you.
Seventy sent. Jesus sends out seventy, two by two, as lambs among wolves, and tells them to say first, at every door: peace be to this house.
Your line: peace be to this house. It was a week of a hidden woman and a waking girl, five loaves, a daily cross, a shining face, a child, a road, and seventy at the door. Another week on the path.

chat.says: When Jesus sent out those seventy, what were they told to say first at a house?
options: Peace be to this house; and if no one receives it, the peace returns to them.
Their message about the kingdom first, then a greeting once they'd been fed.
Nothing at all; they were told to stay silent and simply heal the sick.
